title: Registered Mail
description:
Registered mail in the goshiwon mailbox.

○○ Bank. Addressee: {name}.

'Due to delinquency on the loan of primary debtor Kim ○○,
payment is hereby demanded from you as joint guarantor.
Amount claimed: 32 million won.'

It was one stamp. At a drinking table. Between friends.

This is what Father spent his whole life repaying. Now it was {name}'s turn.

choices.text: Find the friend. First check if he ran
choices.result_text:
The friend hadn't run. He was alone in a half-basement office.

"I'm sorry. Sorry is all I can say."

Heard how the business collapsed. He'd been scammed. Him too.

Drafted a installment repayment agreement together. {name} absorbed part of it.

Thought of Father. That man back then — did he have this same face?

choices.text: Find a lawyer. Reduce it legally first
choices.result_text:
Retainer: 1.5 million won. Worth every won.

"Excess over the maximum legal rate, procedural defects in the acceleration notice — there's room to fight."

32 million won came down to 7 million won. 24 monthly installments.

The lawyer's last words:
"From now on — don't stamp anything, not even at your parents' funeral."

Decided to remember that for life.

title: News About That Friend
description:
The alumni group chat was buzzing.

That friend — the one who asked for the guarantee — his business went under.

Two people had co-signed. Both were on the hook for tens of millions of won.

{name} stared at the screen for a long time.

The friend's expression that night when he refused. The sound of something cracking.
That crack — saved {name}.

choices.text: Reach out. Can't guarantee loans, but can help with other things
choices.result_text:
"Let's get some food."

Met at a gukbap place. The friend couldn't hold eye contact.
"Thank you — for refusing back then. Strange, right? I came out to say that."

At parting, pressed an envelope into his hand. 500,000 won. Not a loan. A gift.

Refused the guarantee, but didn't refuse the friend.
That those are two different things — now they both know.

choices.text: Don't reach out. Distance protects both
choices.result_text:
Wrote several messages. Deleted them all.

Anything sent would read as 'glad it wasn't me.'

The friend quietly left the group chat.

No telling if it was the right call.
Only one thing became certain — that night's refusal was correct.

title: That Building, Auction
description:
A call from the landlord's number — but an unfamiliar man's voice.

"You're the tenant? The building is going to auction. You won't reach the landlord."

The 80% mortgage on the registry. That day's anxiety became reality.

But {name} had a piece of paper.
A jeonse guarantee insurance policy. The 300,000 won paid by skimping on food.

choices.text: File the insurance claim
choices.result_text:
Documents, review, two months.

The full deposit came back.

Other tenants in the building got pushed down the distribution order — most recovered less than half.
The face of the next-door neighbor in the hallway is impossible to forget.

300,000 won. One month of food.
It protected tens of millions.

They say insurance is a losing game.
Correct. Except exactly once.

title: Auction Notice
description:
A notice from the court.

Commencement of voluntary auction proceedings.

The 80% mortgage on the registry — the 80% left to luck that day came back as a blade.

Senior creditors collect first. {name}'s deposit comes after.

Ran the numbers. No matter how — not all of it comes back.

choices.text: Demand for distribution + leasehold registration — recover everything legally possible
choices.result_text:
A month of courts, registry offices, community centers.

Recovered 60% of the deposit through priority repayment and distribution.
The other 40% — 8 million won — vanished.

That day, 300,000 won for insurance felt expensive.
That 300,000 won was actually 8 million won.

Brutal tuition. But this kind of lesson lasts a lifetime after one payment.

choices.text: Track down the landlord personally. Grab him by the collar if needed
choices.result_text:
Went to the landlord's registered address. Already empty.

Learned there that there were seventeen victims.
Joined the class action — but recovery odds were low, they said.

While chasing rage, the distribution demand deadline passed.
Anger ate the procedure.

12 million won. Seoul's lessons always cost this much.

title: There Was No Second Warning
description:
This time it was on the street.

That whiteout feeling — the one from the subway stairs.
That time, he stood up and walked away. Waved people off, said he was fine.

This time, he couldn't get up.

Woke to an emergency room ceiling. IV in his arm.
The doctor looked at the chart. "This isn't your first time, is it."

choices.text: Get the full workup this time
choices.result_text:
Results — overwork, malnutrition, early arrhythmia.

"A few more months of living like this and it would have been serious."

Hospital bill: 1.2 million won. The ER that day would have been 300,000 won.

The body always collects its debts. With interest.

Leaving the hospital, made an appointment for the first time. With himself. Eat, then run.

choices.text: Just take the IV and leave again. Can't stop now
choices.result_text:
The doctor objected. The nurse took a consent form.
'Discharge against medical advice.'

Legs wobbled slightly walking out the hospital door.

A warning ignored twice — isn't a warning the third time.
{name} knew that. Knew it and walked.

Seoul doesn't teach you how to stop.
Until the body teaches you directly.

title: That Lie
description:
Company dinner. The team lead sat down next to {name}, glass in hand.

"You said it at your interview. Six years preparing your own business."

"We're launching a new business initiative — put that experience to use.
Next week, you present to the executives."

Six years. Not a business — repaying debt.
The one line invented in an interview — now had to become presentation slides.

choices.text: Quietly tell the team lead the truth
choices.result_text:
After the second round, pulled the team lead aside.

"The truth is it wasn't a business — I was repaying my father's debt. Six years."

The team lead poured a shot of soju. Said nothing for a while.

"I'll push the presentation. But — a guy who repaid debt for six years beats a guy who prepped a business.
Grit can't be faked."

The lie disappeared. Strangely, leaving something sturdier behind.

choices.text: Study all night and actually pull off the presentation
choices.result_text:
A week of studying business plan formats until 3 AM.

The presentation — passed. An executive nodded.

Walking back, the team lead clapped his shoulder. "Knew you had the experience."

The compliment sat like indigestion.

The lie had become a skill. But the lie hadn't disappeared.
It had just gone deeper.

title: That Night's Answer — Yes
description:
The question came again. No particular reason. At night.

Are you happy?

Answered it once before. That night, the answer was 'yes.'

Time has passed since. The bank account, the body, the people — all different now.

And now?

choices.text: Still yes
choices.result_text:
Not many people can answer 'yes' twice.

{name} knows it isn't because of money.
That night and tonight — the account balance didn't write the answer.

Seoul was outside the window.
One person in this city has said he's happy, twice — right here.

choices.text: ...Now I don't know
choices.result_text:
Back then the answer was yes.

Tallied what had changed. More money than back then. And yet.

Felt like something got left behind somewhere.
Where — finding that became the homework for the time that's left.

title: That Night's Answer — No
description:
The question came again. No particular reason. At night.

Are you happy?

Answered it once before. That night, the answer was 'no.'

Gave that answer and kept running anyway. Didn't stop.

And now?

choices.text: Now — it's a little different
choices.result_text:
Remember the night of answering no.

What happened between then and now?
No major events. Just — endured days, stacking up.

If happiness isn't something that arrives one day
but unhappiness draining out little by little,
then {name} is somewhere in the middle of that now.

That's enough. For today.

choices.text: Still no
choices.result_text:
Same answer the second time.

But this time another question attached itself behind it.

Then — what needs to change?

For the first time, {name} seriously considered
that earning more might not be the answer.

The thought was frightening, so he went to sleep early.
It was still there in the morning.

title: That Night's Answer — Don't Know
description:
The question came again. No particular reason. At night.

Are you happy?

Answered it once before. That night, the answer was 'I don't know.'

'I don't know' was really just a postponed answer.

Time passed, and the postponed question came back with interest.

choices.text: Now there's an answer — yes
choices.result_text:
Wanted to tell the {name} of that night:

Hey. Later, you answer yes to this question.
You won't believe it.

Asked what changed, the explanation doesn't come easily.
Just — at some point, mornings got less heavy.

If that's the definition of happiness, then yes. Happy.

choices.text: Now there's an answer — no
choices.result_text:
'Don't know' became 'no.'

Strangely — it was a relief.

'Don't know' was fog. 'No' is a coordinate.
With a coordinate, you can set a direction.

What's wrong is visible now.
The remaining time is for fixing it.

'No' — turned out to be a usable starting point.

title: What You Said That Day
description:
Sunday night. A call from Father.

"Nothing new. You eating properly?"

The usual script. About to hang up when Father paused a beat.

"...That time at the hospital. You said when you make it to Gangnam, you'd bring me there."

"For me — those words were enough. You really don't have to go.
I called because I was thankful you said it."

choices.text: "I'm going. I'm keeping that promise."
choices.result_text:
A laugh came through the receiver.

"Alright. But don't overdo it. To me, you—"

The words cut off. Long silence.

"...Stay healthy. Hanging up."

Listening to the dial tone, {name} held the phone for a long while.
The unfinished sentence hung somewhere in the line.
To hear the rest of it — he had to go. Gangnam or Changwon.

choices.text: "Father. Even if I never make Gangnam — I'm taking care of you."
choices.result_text:
The other end went quiet.

"...What nonsense. I have a house."

The voice trembled. The pretending was fully audible.

"Hanging up. Eat your meals."

After hanging up, it landed.
Gangnam was a condition, and the condition just got removed.
Remove the condition from a promise — and it becomes a real one.

title: That Classmate, Afterward
description:
A KakaoTalk message. That classmate.

The one who wrapped an arm around his shoulder in the hotel seminar room. Who said 3 million won enrollment.

'Hey. I got out. The day you stormed out — honestly, I started shaking that day.
14 million won in debt left, but I'm out.
Started logistics work. Let's meet. Gukbap's on me.'

choices.text: Go. One bowl of gukbap
choices.result_text:
The gukbap place. The classmate's face was sunburnt but his eyes had returned.

"I saw your expression in that seminar room. The pathetic-look.
That was a mirror. I was making someone else wear that expression too."

Two bowls of gukbap, one bottle of soju.
The classmate paid. 14,000 won.

"Once the debt's cleared, I'll buy you a real drink."
That promise seemed worth believing.

choices.text: Just reply. Distance is still needed
choices.result_text:
'Glad to hear it. You've been through it. Food sometime, for sure.'

Didn't set when sometime was.

The applause from that seminar room still rang in his ears.
Decided not to hate the person. Decided to hate the system.

But separating those two takes time.
The classmate would know that. He'd wait.

title: That Day's 18x
description:
Payday. The number landed in the account.

A month of grinding, converted to money.

But a different number surfaced in his head.
The day the perfecta hit at Gwacheon. Time for 50,000 won to become 900,000 won — two minutes.

One month vs. two minutes.

The moment this comparison begins is the most dangerous moment there is — he'd read that somewhere.

choices.text: Cut the comparison itself. That day was luck
choices.result_text:
Wrote it out on paper.

Won from racing: 900,000 won (once)
Spent on racing: more than that, in total.

The brain remembers only the winning days. The ledger remembers everything.

{name} put the paper in his wallet.
To take out on days Gwacheon calls.

A salary has no two-minute drama. Instead, it comes every month.
That difference is what builds a life.

choices.text: This weekend. Just once more
choices.result_text:
Saturday. Gwacheon. Line 4.

'Just once' became five races. 150,000 won melted.

The memory of 900,000 won was the problem.
As long as that memory exists, 'just once' is a lie.
A lie told to himself. To the easiest mark there is.

On the train home, {name} saw his face in the window.
A familiar expression. Where had he seen it.

— The men at the betting windows. That expression.
